workingTitle: Two quasars heated a vast bubble in the young universe
publicationStatus: Peer-reviewed Nature Astronomy article published 18 November 2026
coreFacts: J1549+1245 is a dual quasar system at redshift 2.37, seen about 2.8 billion years after the Big Bang; its two galaxies are separated by about 19 kiloparsecs.
VLA, ALMA, and SMA observations were modeled across radio and millimeter wavelengths.
A thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich flux decrement detects localized hot gas at 6 sigma and measures (9.7 ± 1.6) × 10^60 ergs of thermal energy.
The thermal energy is 3.6 times the expected hot-gas energy of a 10^13-solar-mass dark matter halo and at least 0.6 percent of the quasar system's lifetime energy output.
A separate roughly 100-kiloparsec feature has a 5-sigma integrated tSZ signature; broader evidence extends toward 600 kiloparsecs.

sources.label: Excess intergalactic heating around a dual quasar system 2.8 Gyr after the Big Bang

sourceStatus: Primary Nature Astronomy article and full author manuscript read; peer review confirmed.
caveats: The tSZ decrement is the measurement; attributing the excess heat to quasar-driven winds is a physically supported interpretation, not a direct movie of an outflow.
The 0.6 percent coupling estimate assumes a 100-million-year quasar lifetime and is a lower limit.
The larger-scale hot-gas feature is separately measured but its exact origin is less certain.
